Only fragments quoted in English in the French entry's source and validation notes were seen in English (“tactical and technical necessities”, “desirable, possible, and realizable”, “the mass will never rule except in abstracto”, “fundamental problem of politics as a science”, “Who says organization, says oligarchy”); the rest of the inline quotations is translated from the French. Original not retrieved.

The sentence “It is organization which gives birth to the dominion of the elected over the electors… Who says organization, says oligarchy” is copied from the English text already given in the French entry; the URL points to the English Internet Archive edition.
The opening phrase “fundamental sociological law of political parties” appears only in French in the French entry and is translated from it. Original not retrieved.

accroche: Robert Michels studies the most democratic parties of his day and finds in them the power of the leaders over their voters.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Who says organization, says oligarchy.” The phrase comes from Robert Michels's book on political parties, published in German in 1911. It is readily turned into a fatality: every democracy would end up confiscated. The text is more precise, and more unsettling, than the slogan.

## Where Michels Looks

Michels, a sociologist of German origin, does not take as his field organizations that call themselves hierarchical. He studies the parties that display the most complete democracy: the socialist parties, foremost among them German social democracy. If oligarchy appears there, where people elect, mandate, and recall, he holds it to be general. His demonstration starts above all from the organization itself, more than from the psychology of the leaders.

## The Mechanism

In the 1915 English translation by Eden and Cedar Paul, he explains that oligarchy depends on “the psychology of the organization itself,” that is, on the “tactical and technical necessities” that result from the consolidation of any disciplined political body. A large party cannot deliberate all together all the time: it delegates, so it has elected officials, full-time staff, speakers. These end up, according to him, dominating those who chose them. He sums it up thus (editors' translation): “It is organization which gives birth to the dominion of the elected over the electors, of the mandataries over the mandators, of the delegates over the delegators. Who says organization, says oligarchy.”

## The Shift

The first misreading is to read these pages as a plea against democracy. Michels writes that the question is not whether ideal democracy is achievable, but “to what extent and in what measure democracy is desirable, possible, and realizable at a given moment.” He thus moves from all or nothing to the question of degree, and sees in it “the fundamental problem of politics as a science.” He also writes that “the mass will never rule except in abstracto”: the ideal and the reality remain distinct, and it is that gap that is his subject.

The second misreading is to take the “law” for a law of physics. It stems from work on parties before 1914: Seymour Martin Lipset described a union that was an exception to it, and Dankwart Rustow judged the argument fallacious. A statement that presents itself as an iron law therefore remains a hypothesis to be tested against the cases where elected officials were controlled, renewed, or overthrown by their base.

What remains is to ask how much control of elected officials by voters a mass organization can bear without ceasing to function.

repere.texte: Michels writes that the “fundamental sociological law of political parties” is formulated thus: “It is organization which gives birth to the dominion of the elected over the electors… Who says organization, says oligarchy.”
repere.source: Robert Michels, Political Parties, trans. Eden and Cedar Paul (1915), Internet Archive

carte.punch: “Who says organization, says oligarchy”: the trap Michels saw in parties.
carte.idee: In 1911, Michels studies the socialist parties and sees elected officials dominating their voters. For him, the cause is above all organization, not merely bad faith: the real question is how far democracy is realizable.

quiz.question: What mechanism does Michels invoke to explain oligarchy in parties?
choix: The corruption of leaders, who betray their platform out of self-interest
The bylaws, which supposedly forbid activists from controlling their elected officials
Delegation, which gives elected officials a power that their voters no longer control
The recruitment of leaders from the aristocracy, which keeps its habits of command
quiz.explication: For Michels, the cause lies above all in organization itself: delegating creates specialists who dominate. He reduces it neither to individual betrayal nor to a rule written in the bylaws.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Michels choose the socialist parties as his field of study?
choix: Their leaders were reputed to be more corrupt than others
If oligarchy appears there despite elections, it is probably general
Their bylaws reserved power to a small committee
They were the only organized parties existing in 1911
quiz_supplementaire.explication: These parties display the most complete democracy: if oligarchy sets in there, where people elect, mandate, and recall, Michels holds it to be general.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What question does Michels ask about democracy?
choix: It is already fully realized in the socialist parties
It is impossible, and so it must be given up
To what extent it is desirable, possible, and realizable
It becomes achievable only once parties are abolished
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Michels shifts the question from all or nothing to degree: to what extent democracy is desirable and realizable at a given moment.
